item: The data files are checked table by table after an unexpected stop, before collection writes again (E2)
key_paths: src/database/verify.py; src/database/damage.py; src/scheduler/storage_guard.py; src/scheduler/runner.py; src/wiki/runner.py; src/api/boot_sequence.py; src/api/main.py; src/static/app-core.js; src/static/taskmanager.js; tests/test_database_verify.py; tests/test_boot_sequence.py; tests/storage_guard_node_test.js; src/backup/merge.py; src/database/connect.py; docs/USER_MANUAL.md; docs/ledger/LESSONS.md; tests/test_database_verify_pages.py; tests/damaged_store_helpers.py
summary: After a session that did not end cleanly (the ledger's clean is False; an unknown end is not a reason) or a check left unfinished (at most 3 starts in a row), the corpus, Wikipedia and law files are read once each, table by table (smallest first by the planner's statistics) with PRAGMA quick_check(table) on its own read-only connection through the one connect() factory, armed in the start-up upkeep before the boot-sequence thread exists and run as its first step. From arming to the end, admit() answers verifying (phase paused-verifying), the Wikipedia lane and off-peak maintenance wait, Resume anyway is refused with its own sentence and the task manager and vitals panel show table N of M; the check always ends (a finally, a disarm when the thread cannot start) and is read once per process. A table is damaged only on a non-ok answer or SQLITE_CORRUPT; busy, locked, I/O error, interrupt, missing file, wrong or missing passphrase and a stop are unchecked with the reason, never damage, and a stopped run leaves the entry running so the next start reads again. A damaged table latches its file through the same _apply_incident a corruption error uses (search-index scope only when every damaged table is the index's). database-damage.json gains a per-file verification block (verdict and seconds per table, page facts, trigger, attempts), carried by the diagnostics member (cut to the verdicts when small). The check is armed as the start-up upkeep's first statement, before its slow steps, and the wait is ended in a finally unless the thread that runs the check was started; a due check is recorded as owed (also by a boot that stays locked), so a session closed before it began does not cancel it, and owing is not an attempt; a damaged verdict survives a restart (the file is read again at every start until it reads clean or is replaced), and an error FTS5 reports as a row (out of memory, I/O, full) is unchecked, never damage. A start of collection (the network toggle going online, a Run now, the Wikipedia lane's start) RE-READS the tables the check reported instead of releasing the latch it set: the claim carries a token and the incident count it was made at, the latch is released only when every reported table reads clean, a failed read that lands while it runs holds the latch, an unread table stays in the set, a (schema) the check could not read means every table is read, and a replaced file (a restore) releases outright and forgets the verdict; the progress shows as table N of M. A boot that starts locked and is then unlocked in the same process plans from the earlier process's record through its own owed entry, so a damaged verdict, an unfinished check and the attempt cap survive the default (encrypted) install's boot. connect() chains the error of the page size that got past page 1. Four new strings x12 (the pause's refusal, the paused phase, the table N of M line, the re-read line) and the three damage sentences (library, search index, hover) reworded x12 to say what a start now does; OO_BOOT_VERIFY is in the manual. Each claim has a test on real damaged copies (plaintext, SQLCipher, FTS5), and the main ones were run against a mutant of their code. Not built: repair and salvage (E3), an operator skip. The check never gives up a finding: the cap of three starts stops RE-RUNNING it, a file an earlier check reported as damaged stays latched from the record (the task manager says the check stopped after N starts) until a re-read of the reported tables comes back clean or the file is replaced, the finding is carried through every record that replaces it, a read that could not happen (busy, no memory, an unreadable table list, a file that cannot be examined) is never a clean read, and a re-read with no claim of its own settles nothing. The check opens each file read-only (mode=ro), so it can no longer be the last connection to close and fold a leftover write-ahead log into the file. (E2b) On an encrypted file, a table whose check raised the driver's generic error is followed by one PRAGMA cipher_integrity_check on a read-only connection, recorded as a (pages) entry (damaged with the lowest 32 page numbers and the full count, ok, or unchecked with the reason); 30 of 40 single damaged pages were filed unchecked before and the pragma named the page in every one tried; measured 1.0 s for 234 MB with no memory beyond the process's own. A main file longer than 4 GiB is not given to that pass (it reads the wrong bytes there: a healthy 4.52 GB file answered a failure for every page from the first past 4 GiB), so it is unchecked with the reason and never called clean; a read-error row whose offset prints negative past 2 GiB is told from damage; the record counts the unknown rows (strange_rows) and keeps pages_unread as a number. (E2 fold 3) A table, the list of tables ((schema)) and the page pass ((pages)) that report damage are read again on a new connection and filed damaged only when the second read agrees (second_read agreed); a second read that is clean or could not be made files the entry unchecked with the first read's first line, the key of what the second read did and the sentence that nothing was concluded, so nothing latches and nothing is repaired on a damage that was not measured twice; an ok or unchecked first read costs one read, and a re-read that settles nothing never replaces an earlier confirmed finding.
